title: Develop Healthy Tech Habits with Your Teen
summary: ‘Scroll Less, Live More’ helps teens and parents develop the tech skills they need to live a life rooted in reality and steeped in wisdom.
summary_zh: “少滚动，多活”可以帮助青少年和家长培养他们所需的技术技能，从而过上扎根于现实、充满智慧的生活。
title_zh: 与青少年一起养成健康的科技习惯
content: Each Sunday night at youth group, our time of worship through singing is followed by a short sermon then small-group discussion. The high school kids in the group I lead know the routine. Before we open the Scriptures, we pull our chairs into a circle. Then we take out our phones and stack them in a pile on the floor in the middle of the ring. We won’t touch those screens again until the Bible-study hour is done. The phone stack is a simple habit. But it’s helped the students in our group pay closer attention to both one another and the Bible text. In his practical new book, Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Healthy Tech Habits for Teens , Samuel James commends a number of similar practices. His goal is to give teenagers “a vivid picture of what it looks like to apply [biblical] wisdom to technology usage in today’s digital age” (155). James recognizes that simple, repeatable practices can help young people resist the foolishness today’s tech promotes so they can instead grow in the fear of the Lord. Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More builds on the foundation James laid in his previous book for adults, Digital Liturgies: Rediscovering Christian Wisdom in an Online Age . One of his main premises is that technology isn’t neutral. Rather, it’s a powerful force that “shapes and influences us in ways we aren’t always aware of” (30). One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. To illustrate this truth, James points to tech invented in the 19th century: Before the telephone . . . people just accepted that if they weren’t in the same room as somebody, they couldn’t communicate with that person in the moment. After the telephone was introduced, being able to communicate with someone in a different place at any time became not only possible but also important. (125) Similarly, 21st-century tech such as generative AI brings with it both new possibilities and greater expectations: “AI’s capability to produce an amazing variety of work and art with very little direct human involvement creates an expectation that using it regularly for these purposes is normal” (127). The more we off-load our creativity and effort to it, the more we believe we should do so. One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. Digital technology changes us in other ways too. James draws on the work of tech realists such as Neil Postman , Nicholas Carr , and Marshall McLuhan , but he makes their perspective accessible for adolescents. James repeatedly shows young people how poor digital habits affect their cognition, emotions, and relationships. Living on a phone will slow down thinking, leaving teens feeling anxious, or even angry, amid daily interactions that then become more awkward and strained. Way of Wisdom: Guard Your Heart How do we help young people avoid this path? James gives teens some practical encouragements, telling them to charge their phones somewhere other than in their bedrooms overnight. He also provides a list self-examination questions to help them grow in self-awareness and he appeals to family rules such as only using devices in open areas of the home. But ultimately, James is convinced that using technology well involves more than simply following a list of dos and don’ts. He writes, We don’t need a huge list of rules that will have to be updated every time Apple releases a new phone or a new social media app; we need something that will help us determine how to use technology well in any circumstance. We need wisdom. (16–17) Proverbs says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight” (9:10). James is clear that growing in wisdom and the knowledge of the Lord requires more than adjusting one’s screen-time settings; it takes guarding one’s heart. James encourages teens to think of their hearts as a palace where a king or queen lives. title: Effective Altruists and the Spreadsheet Gospel
summary: Effective altruism commands us to love our neighbor yet dissolves that neighbor into a statistic. It asks for the fruit of the image of God while denying the root.
summary_zh: 有效的利他主义命令我们爱我们的邻居，但却把那个邻居溶解成一个统计数字。它要求上帝形象的果实，同时否认根源。
title_zh: 有效的利他主义者和电子表格福音
content: Over the past decade, an emergent secular philosophy has taken root in Silicon Valley. It now drives many conversations around politics and technology, particularly as its ideas shape how our society approaches artificial intelligence. Known as “effective altruism,” this worldview is having a moment. The Economist recently called the philosophy “this century’s biggest idea” and labeled the movement as “admirable, but dangerous.” Even as this philosophy is moving markets and shaping global debates, many Christians are unfamiliar with it. As a Christian and tech-policy analyst based in Washington, DC, where many of these conversations are taking place, I want to explain what effective altruism is, examine what it promises and where it fails to deliver, and show why this budding movement is incongruent with and a poor substitute for the gospel. What Is Effective Altruism? Effective altruism emerged in the late 2000s and early 2010s from the convergence of several intellectual movements, particularly utilitarian philosophy and evidence-based philanthropy. Australian academic Peter Singer provided an important foundation with his 1972 essay “ Famine, Affluence and Morality ,” where he argues that people have a moral obligation to prevent suffering when they can do so at relatively little cost to themselves. At its core, effective altruism is consequentialist, judging the rightness of an action chiefly by its outcomes. The tenets of effective altruism are straightforward: People should use reason, logic, and personal resources to maximize the good they do in society. The Centre for Effective Altruism explains , “We’re committed to prioritizing actions that benefit more lives over actions that benefit a few—that saving a billion lives is more important than saving ten.” The tenets of effective altruism are straightforward: People should use reason, logic, and personal resources to maximize the good they do in society. The movement took shape with the founding of several philanthropic organizations, such as GiveWell and 80,000 Hours . These groups emphasize measuring charitable impact, directing money toward the most effective actions, and choosing “high-impact” careers based on their potential to do good. Their approach to charitable giving has produced endeavors to improve global health , animal welfare , and economic disparities , among other areas. Over the past decade, effective altruism has expanded its scope, focusing on posterity and “longtermism,” the belief that “positively influencing the longterm future is a key moral priority of our time.” The Economist notes a belief this leads to: “Those not born yet should be weighed in the balance—and there could be trillions of them. Many EAs are ‘longtermists’ who feel bound to forestall risks in the distant future, even if that starves today’s good causes, such as helping the desperately poor.” This belief manifests itself in a focus on concerns such as existential risk (e.g., climate change or the next pandemic), nuclear proliferation, and artificial intelligence. For many in Silicon Valley, advanced AI is the defining problem of our day. The concern about a potential AI apocalypse explains why the movement has invested heavily in AI research, AI companies, and AI advocacy and safety. It’s not difficult to see why this philosophy has a natural audience among AI researchers and Silicon Valley tech luminaries. Effective altruism enables technologists to approach ethics in a way that can feel familiar: a series of probabilities, tradeoffs, and expected results—measuring an individual’s moral standing as mathematic calculations, similar to the process of building a software program where different inputs result in varied outputs. For ambitious individuals accustomed to solving complicated projects through ingenuity and critical analysis, this movement delivers reassuring community in an industry that often feels isolating. 在过去十年中,一种新兴的世俗哲学在硅谷生根. 它现在推动了许多关于政治和技术的对话,特别是它的思想决定了我们社会如何对待人工智能。 这种世界观被称作“有效的利他主义”,它正在有一个时刻。

经济学人最近称这个哲学是“本世纪最大的思想 ” , 并称这个运动为“可喜但危险的 ” 。 即使这种哲学正在推动市场和形成全球辩论,许多基督徒对它并不熟悉。

作为总部设在华盛顿特区的基督教和技术政策分析者,我想解释一下这些对话是何等有效的利他主义,审视它所承诺的以及它未能兑现之处,并表明为什么这个萌芽的运动与福音不相干,并且是一个糟糕的代名词。 什么是有效的替代主义?

2000年代后期和2010年代初,有效的利他主义从几个知识运动,特别是功利主义哲学和以证据为基础的慈善活动趋同而出.

澳大利亚学者彼得·辛格以他1972年的论文"饥荒,富裕和道德"为重要基础,他在该作中认为,当人们能够以相对较少的代价来预防痛苦时,他们有道德义务. 有效的利他主义的核心是结果主义,主要根据其结果判断行动是否正确。

有效的利他主义原则是直截了当的:人们应该利用理性、逻辑和个人资源来最大限度地发挥其在社会中的效益。

“有效替代主义中心”解释说,“我们致力于优先考虑有利于更多生命的行动,而不是有利于少数人的行动——拯救十亿生命比拯救十亿生命更重要。 ” 有效的利他主义原则是直截了当的:人们应该利用理性、逻辑和个人资源来最大限度地发挥其在社会中的效益。

随着几个慈善组织的成立, 这些团体强调衡量慈善影响,将资金用于最有效的行动,并根据他们做好事的潜力选择“高影响”职业。

他们的慈善捐赠方法 带来了改善全球卫生、动物福利和经济差距的努力。

在过去的十年中,有效的利他主义扩大了它的范围,把重点放在后人和“长期主义”上,认为“积极影响长期的未来是我们时代的主要道德优先事项”。 《经济学家》指出,这导致了一种信念:“那些尚未出生的,应该加以权衡,而且可能有上万亿美元。

许多职业介绍所是“长期主义者 ” , 他们认为他们有义务在遥远的将来预防风险, 即使这饿死今天的好原因, 这种信念表现在关注存在风险(如气候变化或下个大流行病)、核扩散和人工智能等关注。

对硅谷的许多人来说,先进的AI是我们当今的决定性问题. 对AI可能启示录的担忧解释了为什么该运动在AI研究、AI公司以及AI的倡导和安全方面投入了大量资金. 为何这个哲学在AI研究人员和硅谷科技流派中有自然的读者,

title: New Free Playlist: 30 Songs of Gratitude to God
summary: Brett McCracken curates a playlist of 30 songs to help you practice gratitude to God—not just on Thanksgiving but every day.
summary_zh: 布雷特·麦克拉肯（ Brett McCracken ）策划了一个包含30首歌曲的播放列表，以帮助您不仅在感恩节，而且每天都对上帝表示感谢。
title_zh: 新的免费播放列表： 30首感谢上帝的歌曲
content: The older I get, the more convinced I am that a posture of gratitude is key to a life of joy. God’s gifts are constant and abundant—his daily provision of life and breath far more than we deserve. Being alert to the constancy of his gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention . That’s why Thanksgiving is such a great holiday. It’s at least one day dedicated to pausing and taking stock, giving our attention to the Giver of all good gifts. Being alert to the constancy of God’s gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention. But it’s a shame Thanksgiving is just one day. Because really, we should practice gratitude constantly. What if, as a start, we dedicated the whole month of November to giving thanks? What if we dedicated time each day this month to intentionally naming God’s provision and giving him thanks? To help, I created a new playlist all about giving thanks to God. The playlist has 30 songs (one for each of November’s 30 days) expressing gratitude to God for our salvation in Christ, for the many blessings of marriage and family, and for the beauty of the earth. You can access the playlist now on Spotify and Apple Music . Enjoy! title: The Voice of the Martyrs: Prayers of the Persecuted
summary: We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners.
summary_zh: 我们祈求正义，但我们是作为被饶恕的罪人祈求正义。
title_zh: 殉道者的声音：受迫害者的祈祷
content: “How long, O LORD? . . . Pour out your anger. . . . Let the avenging of the outpoured blood of your servants be known among the nations before our eyes!” (Ps. 79:5–6, 10). As you’re reading through Psalms and you stumble across Psalm 79, you can’t help but wonder what to do with this very Old Testament-sounding prayer. Surely, Asaph needed to be educated in the gospel, right? Revelation 6:9–10 describes the martyrs in heaven who have been slain for their testimony to the gospel and places Psalm 79 on their lips: “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” Scholars agree the prayer of Psalm 79 is the likely background for the prayer of the martyrs, furthering our appreciation of this as a prayer for the church. It’s a prayer of and for the persecuted church. As we stand alongside them, we have divine warrant to pray Psalm 79 on their behalf. Trevor Laurence explains , “The vengeance petition of Rev. 6:9–10 thus supplies a model for the ongoing prayer of Christ’s body on earth.” Rather than being contrary to New Testament ethics, then, Psalm 79 fuels the church’s longing for every wrong to be made right. Nevertheless, you may still wonder, How do I take up a psalm like this in prayer for my persecuted brothers and sisters without falling into vindictive rage and vengefulness? Thankfully, Psalm 79 provides the guidelines needed to answer this question. Pray in Response to Horrific Injustice Verses 1–4 catalog the horrors God’s people suffered at the hands of the Babylonians who destroyed their temple: They defiled God’s holy place, they gave the flesh of God’s faithful ones to the beasts of the earth, they poured out their blood like water and refused them a proper burial, and they were the cause of God’s people becoming a taunt to their neighbors. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. This has two implications. First, these prayers do not give license for us to pray such things against just anyone. Second, if we object to such prayers, they challenge us to ask whether we have ever faced anything close to the agonizing evil that gave birth to this prayer. As Jamie Grant posits , “Perhaps our reluctance to appropriate the psalms of enmity is rooted in the comfort of our lives.” If we knew the kind of horror Psalm 79 speaks of (and that our persecuted brothers and sisters endure daily), perhaps we wouldn’t be so quick to dismiss these psalms. Pray for the Glory of God As psalms like this respond to such evil, they are fundamentally concerned with God’s glory. We see this in Psalm 79:6, where the nations’ refusal to call on God’s name is the motive behind Asaph’s cry. Likewise, verse 9 cites the glory of God’s name and his “name’s sake” as a rationale for God to answer this request. And verse 10 is concerned that, at present, the onlooking nations say, “Where is their God?” So Asaph asks that God’s justice would be made known among the nations (v. 10), and that God’s people might praise him for it (v. 13). The glory of God is the ultimate end of the imprecatory psalms. Or as James Hamilton says , “The glory of God in salvation through judgment is the center of the theology of Psalms.” The same is true of imprecatory psalms like Psalm 79. Their controlling desire is “Hallowed be thy name.” Pray with a Humble Posture The imprecatory psalms are not prayed in a spirit of self-righteousness; those praying them understand their need for God’s grace. They pray for justice from a posture of humility, where they confess that this judgment is what they too deserve apart from God’s grace (vv. 8–9). This is not unlike the widow’s prayer for justice in Luke 18:1–8 being paired with the parable of the Pharisee and tax collector in verses 9–14. We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners. title: Martin Luther in 5 Latin Phrases
summary: Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift.
summary_zh: 耶稣完美的生命和牺牲的死亡对所有信徒都很重要。因此，神的义不仅仅是他的审判。这也是他的天赋。
title_zh: 马丁·路德的5个拉丁短语
content: Martin Luther was born in Eisleben, Germany, on November 10, 1483. He was christened at Saints Peter and Paul Church the next day. At age 7, Luther entered the Mansfeld Latin School. There he learned Latin grammar and prayers, and he memorized Aesop’s Fables . From those early years through his time studying at boarding school in Magdeburg then later at the University of Erfurt, Luther was a diligent student. He kept up with his Latin, and several important Latin phrases appear throughout Luther’s writings. Five of them serve as a good summary of his life and chief theological emphases. 1. Iustitia Dei In July 1505, Luther was caught in a fierce thunderstorm. Panicked and terrified, he bargained with God, promising to become a monk. After entering the monastery, Luther was again overcome by fear. When he led his first mass as a priest, it wasn’t an occasion of joy. Instead, it was filled with trembling. As the service began, Luther took his place at the front of the chapel, and he began to recite the Latin prayers. Luther knew that God is perfect in judgment and completely without sin. So as he thought about iustitia Dei , “the righteousness of God” (Rom. 1:17), terror struck him. Biographer Roland H. Bainton describes the thoughts that plagued Luther’s mind: Who am I that I should . . . raise my hands to the divine Majesty? The angels surround him. At his nod the earth trembles . . . [but] I am dust and ashes. When Luther held up the bread and wine, he shook so badly he almost dropped the cup. During those years growing up in school and at the monastery, Luther only thought of God’s righteousness, or justice, as his active judgment against human sin. He later wrote , Though I lived as a monk without reproach, I felt and knew I was a sinner before God. I had an extremely disturbed conscience. . . . I hated the righteous God who punishes sinners. 2. Extra nos In 1512, Luther became a university professor in Wittenberg. As he studied the Bible for his lectures, he began to see God’s righteousness in a new light. Luther saw how Jesus Christ took on our humanity, how he lived a perfect life and died the painful and shameful death of the cross to take the punishment due for sin. He saw how God raised Jesus from the dead, and how he now justifies Christians by faith. God declares that in his sight, Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift of salvation. Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift. What happened when Luther made this discovery? Here’s how he described it: “I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates.” After that day, Luther began to teach that God gives Christians his “alien righteousness,” that is, a righteousness that comes extra nos , “from outside of us.” Our righteousness isn’t from us; it doesn’t come from what we do. It can’t be earned by saying a prayer or even by having a good attitude. Our righteousness is ultimately found in and belongs to another, our Savior Jesus Christ. 3. Crux sola est nostra theologia On October 31, 1517, Luther famously posted his Ninety-five Theses on the door of Castle Church. In it, Luther spoke clearly against the money-raising indulgence schemes Pope Leo X and Germany’s own Prince Albert of Brandenburg had sponsored. The next year, in April 1518, Luther defended these views at the Augustinian order’s spring meeting in Heidelberg. Luther walked to the meeting in fear. He expected the leaders there to sternly rebuke him. After all, that’s what the pope had asked them to do. But to Luther’s surprise, the leaders at the meeting welcomed his defense with excitement. content_zh: 马丁·路德于1483年11月10日生于德国艾斯莱本. 第二天他在圣彼得和保罗教堂被洗礼. 7岁时,路德进入了曼斯菲尔德拉丁学校. 他在那里学习了拉丁语的语法和祷告,并记住了艾索普的"寓言". 从早年到后来在马格德堡的寄宿学校学习,路德是一名勤奋的学生。 他跟上了拉丁语,几个重要的拉丁语短语也出现在路德的著作中. 其中5个是他的生平和首席神学重心的良好总结. 1. Iustitia Dei 1505年7月,路德被猛烈的雷暴所困. 惊慌惊恐地与上帝讨价还价,许诺成为和尚. 进入修道院后,路德再次被恐惧所克服. 当他第一次作为牧师主持弥撒时, 相反,充满了颤抖。 随着礼拜的开始,路德在礼拜堂前取而代之,他开始背诵拉丁语祈祷. 路德知道上帝在判断上是完美的,并且完全没有罪恶. 因此,当他想到了iustitia Dei“上帝的公义”(1:17)时,恐怖袭击了他。 传记家罗兰·H·班顿(Roland H. Bainton)描述了困扰路德思想的思想:我该向神圣的陛下举起手来, 众天神围绕他. 在他点头的时候,大地会颤抖... ...但是,我是灰尘和灰烬。 当路德拿起面包和葡萄酒时,他摇得这么厉害,差点把杯子掉下. 在那些年里,路德在学校和修道院里长大,他只把上帝的正义或正义视为他对人类罪恶的积极判断。 他后来写道, 虽然我作为一个和尚生活 没有责备, 我感觉和知道我是上帝面前的罪人。 我有一个极度不安的良心。 我憎恨惩罚罪人的善良之神 2. 1512年,路德成为维滕贝格的大学教授. 当他为他的演讲而学习圣经时,他开始在新的光芒下看到上帝的正义. 路德看到耶稣基督如何对待我们的人性,他如何过上完美的生活并死于十字架上的痛苦而可耻的死亡来取取罪的惩罚. 他看见了上帝如何使耶稣从死地复活,以及他现在如何通过信仰为基督徒辩护. 上帝宣布,在他看来,耶稣的完美生活和牺牲的死亡对所有信徒都很重要。 因此上帝的正义不仅仅是他的判断。 这也是他的救赎天赋。 耶稣的完美生活和牺牲的死亡是所有信徒的计数. 因此上帝的正义不仅仅是他的判断。 这也是他的天赋。 当路德做出这个发现时发生了什么? 他是这样描述的 : “ 我感到我再次出生,并通过开放的大门进入了天堂。 ” 在那一天之后,路德开始教导上帝给予基督徒“外星人的正义 ” , 即“来自我们以外的”一种格外不义的正义。 我们的正义不是来自我们, 祈祷, 我们的正义最终被发现 并属于另一个,我们的救主耶稣基督。 3. Crux sola est nostra Godologia 1517年10月31日,路德将他的"95个本事"出名地贴在了城堡教堂的门上. 路德在书中明确表示反对教皇利奥十世和德国自己的勃兰登堡阿尔贝特亲王赞助的集资宽恕计划。 次年,即1518年4月,路德在海德堡举行的奥古斯丁会令春季会议上为这些观点辩护. 路德在恐惧中走去开会. 他期望那里的领导人严厉斥责他。 这毕竟是教皇要求他们做的。 但令路德惊讶的是,与会领导人激动地欢迎他的辩护. 路德怎么说 他的新朋友这么兴奋? 路德在他的"海德堡争论"中描述了两类人——"荣耀之神"和"十字架之神". 这个

title: ‘Mosquito Bowl’: Football Stars on the Front Lines
summary: Peter Berg’s ‘The Mosquito Bowl’ is essentially ‘Friday Night Lights’ meets ‘Hacksaw Ridge.’
summary_zh: Peter Berg的“The Mosquito Bowl”本质上是“周五夜灯”与“Hacksaw Ridge”相遇。
title_zh: “蚊子碗” ：前线的足球明星
content: Peter Berg’s The Mosquito Bowl is essentially Friday Night Lights meets Hacksaw Ridge . It’s a movie with the same creative vibe as Friday Night Lights (gritty handheld camera, muted color palette, Explosions in the Sky post-rock soundtrack) but applied to a brutally violent true story of WWII’s Battle of Okinawa, one of the single bloodiest battles of the 20th century. Also like Berg’s Friday Night Lights , The Mosquito Bowl ( out now in theaters ; coming to Netflix November 25) is based on a book by Pulitzer Prize–winning journalist Buzz Bissinger . The 2022 book—subtitled A Game of Life and Death in World War II —only has one chapter (of 41) devoted to the actual 1944 football game dubbed “The Mosquito Bowl.” Most of the book is about the war, and the young men who left wives, kids, and promising NFL careers to fight it. Likewise, Berg’s film adaptation is mostly a somber, unflinching WWII film, with a brief reprieve of joy in the form of a football game on Guadalcanal between the 4th and 29th regiments of the 6th Marine Division. Just as in Friday Night Lights , where the drama of high school football parallels the struggles and triumphs of life off the field, the football game in The Mosquito Bowl parallels the “game of life and death” that surrounds the men at war. Sports are interesting in this way: They provide escape from real life but also training for it, an arena of danger and high stakes but not ultimate stakes. Sports often map onto life—we draw up plans and plays but have to improvise; we get hurt but can heal; we thrive individually through teamwork; sometimes we win and sometimes we lose. Yet sports are unlike real life too. Winning or losing on the field is a matter of trophies and glory, but off the field, it can be a matter of life and death. Young Men Willing to Fight and Die The Mosquito Bowl (rated R for graphic war violence and language), opens with a well-known epigraph from Herbert Hoover : Older men declare war. But it is youth that must fight and die. And it is youth who must inherit the tribulation, the sorrow, and the triumphs that are the aftermath of war. This is a movie about youth—or rather, the passage from youth into adulthood that war accelerates. This is a movie about youth—or rather, the passage from youth into adulthood that war accelerates. The movie opens with muddy college football scenes in the fall of 1941, as the four central characters are introduced: John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Brown quarterback; Bob Baumann (Bill Skarsgård), University of Wisconsin tackle; Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson), Purdue fullback; and Dave Schreiner (Tom Francis), Wisconsin end. They were all-star athletes with promising futures. Many of them were collegiate All-Americans and drafted by NFL teams. Yet December 7, 1941, happened, and their futures were all changed. Once bound together by football skill, friendly rivalry, and fierce competition on the gridiron, these men soon bonded in a different setting: as marines in WWII’s savage Pacific theater. Instead of fighting for yards on the field, they fought for ground in a war of attrition on Okinawa. Instead of a football in hand, they carried guns and bayonets. Instead of tackling their opponents, they wrestled them to the death in hand-to-hand combat. Like many in the Greatest Generation, these men volunteered to enlist and fight. The Mosquito Bowl celebrates their duty and sacrifice. In one scene, Baumann’s younger brother says, “You don’t have to go,” to which Baumann replies, “I do. I’m needed.” It’s hard to imagine star athletes, whether collegiate or professional, volunteering to go to war in 2026. But in 1943, it was normal. Okinawa, Bissinger writes in the book, was “by far the largest collection of athletes ever to die in a single battle.” And in the entirety of WWII, 21 NFL players died in combat, as well as two players from Major League Baseball. title: Pastor, Be Opportunistic
summary: Pastor, you cannot afford to coast. You cannot afford autopilot. Be a gospel entrepreneur. Eternity is at stake.
summary_zh: 牧师，您负担不起海岸。您买不起自动驾驶仪。成为一名福音企业家。永恒岌岌可危。
title_zh: 牧师，抓住机会
content: My coffee had gone cold as the church planter mourned that his church felt stagnant. Worse than not growing—a thick malaise had settled over the congregation. The first three years were exciting; the community was intrigued by a new church plant, genuinely curious about what it was all about. But everything had plateaued. Leaders grew complacent. Sundays—even with strong preaching—felt cold and passionless. The church’s reason for existing had shrunk to feeding and caring for the Christians who already called it home. The church planter couldn’t see how it was still transforming the community. An older mentor at the table cleared his throat. “I’m sorry to hear that. Let me ask you—what is one risky, hard thing the Lord is inviting your church to do that you’re hesitant to do?” The planter scratched his head. “I don’t know. I’ve never been asked that before.” The older man shrugged. “Every pastor should be ready to answer that question. If he can’t, he needs to spend some time praying and fasting until he can. Comfort and complacency are incredibly dangerous.” I’ve sat in enough of these conversations to know that wise, healthy risks are vital to the life of the church. Without them, the church atrophies. Its reason for existing collapses into self-care and, after a few years, into self-preservation. Risky and hard things keep gospel blood flowing through the body. Pastor, you cannot afford to coast. You cannot afford autopilot. You owe it to Jesus and to your church to make the most of opportunities in your city—which means that alongside preaching, teaching, praying, and developing leaders, you need to prioritize seeking new avenues for ministry. Be a gospel entrepreneur. Church-planting networks have long understood that entrepreneurial aptitude is essential for planters. But what about established churches—do their pastors need to be entrepreneurial too? What Is a Gospel Entrepreneur? There’s still hesitancy around saying pastors need entrepreneurial aptitude. Maybe it’s because we picture someone who constantly starts new things he can’t sustain—a person with a billion ideas who follows through on none of them. If this is what we mean, then no, we don’t want our pastors to be entrepreneurial. Comfort and complacency are incredibly dangerous. But a gospel entrepreneur is something different. He doesn’t pile up harebrained ideas. He stays awake and sober-minded about the opportunities the Lord is opening in the community. He sees the wooden frames of a new development and prays about how the gospel will reach those families once they move in. He looks at neighborhoods where existing churches can’t possibly reach everyone—and plants a church there. He saves, scrimps, and sacrifices to move a growing church plant into a more strategic location. He keeps his eyes open, his mind sharp, and his hands ready for the moment God opens a door. Biblical Call When this topic comes up, someone usually asks, “Where do you see the need for a pastor to be an entrepreneur in the Bible?” My answer often surprises people: Jesus’s parable of the dishonest manager. In Luke 16:1–9, a rich man discovers his property manager has been wasting his possessions and tells him to settle accounts—he’s about to be fired. The manager realizes losing his job means either digging or begging, so he immediately goes to work cutting deals to gain favor with other wealthy employers. When his employer finds out, he commends the manager for his shrewdness. Ethical or not, it was a genius move. At this point, we should ask, Why is Jesus telling this story? Maybe he’s about to indict people like the manager. But the manager’s dishonesty has nothing to do with Jesus’s point. The twist is that Jesus holds up the dishonest manager as an example of what he wants his disciples to be. “The master commended the dishonest manager for his shrewdness,” Jesus says. “For the sons of this world are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than the sons of light” (Luke 16:

title: The Dangers of Getting Advice from the Internet
summary: Melissa and Courtney discuss how to cultivate discernment when seeking advice online and recognize the danger of letting AI or influencers replace wise counsel from the body of Christ.
summary_zh: Melissa和Courtney讨论了如何在网上寻求建议时培养洞察力，并认识到让人工智能或影响者取代基督身体的明智建议的危险。
title_zh: 从互联网上获取建议的危险
content: Melissa and Courtney discuss how to cultivate discernment when seeking advice. They talk about how sometimes we think we need information when what we really need is relationship. They discuss what kind of advice they like to get from the internet or ChatGPT, why they don’t recommend it for wisdom issues such as marriage and parenting, and why we shouldn’t let advice from AI or influencers replace wise counsel from the body of Christ. Resource Mentioned: Kitchen-Table Counseling Within Your Local Church Related Resources: Let’s Talk: Finding a Mentor and Being a Mentor Want to Grow in Wisdom? You Need Gospel Friends. Why AI Parenting Advice Falls Short Don’t Treat AI as Your Pastor Discussion Questions: 1. When you face a difficult decision or struggle, where do you typically turn for advice? 2. How do you discern whether online advice is helpful or unwise? 3. What makes advice offered within a personal relationship different from advice taken from an online blog or influencer or generated by AI? 4. How might repeated exposure to ideas about marriage, parenting, or relationships on social media influence our thinking without us being aware of it? 5. What do we lose when we turn to online sources for counsel instead of investing in relationships with people who know and love us? 6. Who in your life knows you well enough to speak honestly into your decisions and loves you enough to do so? How can you cultivate those kinds of relationships? 7. How would you like to grow in your ability to offer wise counsel to others?

title: Beware Making Mental Illness an Identity
summary: ‘All in Your Head’ is a concrete and compelling remapping of mental health culture with impressive explanatory power.
summary_zh: “All in Your Head”是对心理健康文化的具体而引人注目的重新映射，具有令人印象深刻的解释力。
title_zh: 小心让精神疾病成为一种身份
content: In the years since he was involuntarily committed to a mental health institution for bipolar disorder, Frederik deBoer has wrestled with both profound gratitude for a system that saved his life and also palpable frustration that his experience of healing has become so rare. All in Your Head: Illness as Identity, Trauma as Fashion, and the Desire to Be Disordered is the latest broadside from one of the internet’s most heterodox thinkers and writers. As an “old school” Marxist best known for writing The Cult of Smart , deBoer takes aim at how the cultural drift within his own tribe is responsible for making mental health care so elusive for those who need it most: “The tendency to treat mental illness as an exciting adventure, the endless romanticization of lunacy in popular culture, is one of many aggravations I have nursed for years” (8). The root of his aggravation—the treatment of mental illness and disability as an identity to be celebrated rather than a disability that needs treatment —isn’t all in his head. The use of talk therapy rose 47 percent between 2019 and 2024 . A 2025 LifeStance survey found around 29 percent of U.S. adults have self-diagnosed their mental health condition after consuming online content, rising to 50 percent among Gen Z (versus 9 percent of boomers). Of the people who self-diagnose symptoms, almost a quarter (24 percent) “rarely” or “never” feel the need to take the next step to discuss them with a qualified clinician. DeBoer argues that rather than reducing the stigma surrounding mental illness, the inordinate attention given to the mildly and dubiously afflicted is a dangerous distraction crowding out help for the severely ill. Accelerated by social media, this “gentrification of disability” has become a full-blown social contagion, compromising even the experts and institutions responsible for mental health care (153–54). DeBoer is largely right, and the cultural shift he identifies has real-world implications both inside and outside the church. But the same ideological priors that so sharpen deBoer’s critique also suffer from two significant blind spots that, were they addressed, would make All in Your Head the more courageous, more constructive, and, therefore, more widely read manifesto we need. General Bipartisan Ire If you picked up All in Your Head to understand how modern therapy culture spread like wildfire across social media over the last several years, it’s not immediately obvious why deBoer starts his argument with an in-depth analysis of the anti-psychiatry movement’s influence in late 20th century politics and academia. But, if you can forgive me the pun, there’s a method to his madness. After a blistering critique of “rightwing libertarian” policies that neglected mental illness, he cashes in on the subsequent trust he earns with left-leaning readers to launch a series of absolute haymakers toward “a species of thought that sometimes amounts to a kind of leftist pseudo-radicalism or a libertarian fantasy” (198) that drives the “destabilizing . . . move from mental illness as reality to mental illness as symbol” (8). American individualism and anti-institutional bias aren’t new, but the painstakingly specific way deBoer traces their spread through the culture surrounding mental health and therapy is refreshing and instructive. Our “apolitical romanticism of resistance to modern society” fuels two opposite errors: On the right, mental illness is sometimes seen as either imagined or a symptom of weak character. But on the left, the same romanticism often describes mental disability as more en abling than dis abling, as if neurodivergent minorities don’t need society’s help—society needs theirs. Gentrification of Disability DeBoer’s emphatic rejection of this predominantly progressive error— of “making a medical disorder an identity”—is the “overarching principle of [his] book” (165). This is never more clear in what he labels “the gentrification of disability,” where “diagnoses bec
content_zh: 在他非自愿地被送入精神病院治疗两极分化后的几年里,弗雷德里克·德·博尔带着对挽救他生命的系统深表感谢和明显的沮丧,因为他的治愈经验变得如此罕见. 在你的脑海中:作为身份的疾病,作为时尚的创伤,以及希望陷入混乱,是互联网上最异形的思想家和作家之一的最新一面。 作为一位最以写作"聪明的邪教"而出名的"老派"马克思主义者,德博尔以自己的部落内部的文化漂移为目的,让那些最需要的人如此难以接受精神保健:"将精神疾病视为激动人心的冒险的倾向,在流行文化中无休止地浪漫化的放荡,是多年来我所照顾的诸多恶化之一"(8). 他的病情恶化的根源——将精神疾病和残疾视为一种值得庆贺的身份,而不是需要治疗的残疾——并不是他脑子里所有的东西。 2019年至2024年间,谈话疗法的使用率上升了47%. 2025年生活稳定调查发现,约29%的美国成年人在消费了在线内容后自行诊断出自己的心理健康状况,在Gen Z中上升到了50%(相对于9%的繁荣者). 在自我诊断的人群中,近四分之一(24%)的人“勉强”或“从未”感到有必要采取下一步措施,与合格的临床医生讨论这些症状。 DeBoer认为,对受轻度和可疑折磨的人的过度关注,与其减少精神疾病的污名化,不如说是一种危险的分心,挤出对重病患者的帮助。 社交媒体加速了这种 " 残疾意识化 " ,已成为一种全面的社会传染,甚至损害负责精神保健的专家和机构(153-54)。 DeBoer基本上是正确的,他所认定的文化转变在教堂内外都具有现实世界的影响. 但德布尔批评如此尖锐的意识形态前科也遭遇了两个重大盲点,如果这些盲点得到解决,将使你的头脑更加勇敢,更具建设性,因此,我们需要更广泛地阅读宣言。 一般两党爱尔兰人 如果你在脑海中看到现代治疗文化在过去几年里如何像野火一样在社交媒体上传播,那么DeBoer为什么以深入分析20世纪后期反精神病运动在政治和学术界的影响为出发点,这并不明显。 但是,如果你能原谅我的双关语,他疯狂是有办法的。 在对忽视了精神疾病的“右翼自由派”政策猛烈批评后,他依靠后来与左翼读者获得的信任,发动了一系列绝对的干草人,走向“有时相当于一种左翼伪激进主义或自由派幻想的思想”(198年),这种思想驱使“从精神疾病变成现实,转变为精神疾病作为象征”(8)。 美国的个人主义和反机构偏见并非新事物, 但DeBoer通过精神卫生与治疗的文化, 我们“反对现代社会的政治浪漫主义”助长了两个相反的错误: 在右边,精神疾病有时被视为一种想象或一种弱性症状. 但是在左边,同样的浪漫主义常常将精神残疾描述为比分身更困难,仿佛神经分身的少数民族不需要社会的帮助——社会需要他们的帮助。 对DeBoer残疾人的强烈反对,即 " 使医疗障碍成为身份 " 这一主要进步的错误,是 " 书中的首要原则 " (165)。 这在他所称的“残疾的基因化”中再清楚不过了。
author: Brad Edwards

title: How a Former Prisoner in Iran Wants You to Pray for Christians in Chains
summary: Pray not only for what God might do for Christian prisoners in Iran but for what God might do through them, for his glory.
summary_zh: 不仅祈求神可以为伊朗的基督徒囚犯做些什么，而且祈求神可以通过他们为祂的荣耀做些什么。
title_zh: 伊朗前囚犯如何希望你为被锁的基督徒祈祷
content: Not long ago, I had a surreal phone call with two young Christian men serving prison sentences in one of Iran’s hardest prisons. They’re there because they refuse to stop preaching about Jesus. When I asked how I could pray for them, their answer wasn’t what you might expect. “Pray that we would not be released until our job here is finished,” they said. They had led numerous fellow prisoners to faith. Now, their chief concern was to remain inside long enough to disciple them. The call took me straight back to the five years I spent in prison for my faith. Now, these dear brothers (let’s call them Vahid and Reza) were behind bars, and I was outside. As we spoke, I pictured the wards and corridors, imagined the sounds and smells, and remembered how hard it was not to know how many years I would be there. But it was also an encouraging call. Vahid and Reza were in high spirits, talking about Bible passages that were sustaining them and how the Lord was at work. They didn’t see themselves in a miserable, dark place. They saw themselves in a different mission field. Their focus was the same as Paul’s in Colossians 4:3: “Pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison.” Paul’s request wasn’t for an open prison door but for an open door for the gospel. Pray for Gospel Fruit Vahid and Reza’s request resonated with me. I remember being unable to pray for my own release. I tried on a few occasions, but I couldn’t open my mouth to ask the Lord to release me. If I’m following Christ, I cannot choose the path. I cannot choose the location. I should follow him wherever he goes. And as I followed him to prison, he brought beautiful fruit. They didn’t see themselves in a miserable, dark place. They saw themselves in a different mission field. I think of one prisoner, a devout Muslim, who was wrongly accused of spying for Iran’s enemies. He was praying he would be released and was frustrated to get no answer. He approached me one day, saying, “Farshid, our God is dead. But I’ve heard yours is alive. Will you pray for me?” Fearing it might be a trap, I took him quietly aside and prayed briefly in the name of Jesus: “Lord, you know this man. Please hear his prayer.” The very next day, the man rushed over excitedly and gave me a huge hug. That morning, he had learned his name had been cleared. He was released two weeks later. Our God is indeed alive. The Lord was also at work softening my parents’ hearts toward Christ during those years. I always say that even if only for the salvation of my parents, my time in prison was worth it. So, when you pray for persecuted believers, pray not only for what God might do for them but—as Vahid and Reza requested—for what God might do through them, for his glory. Pray for gospel fruit. Pray for Comfort and Endurance I don’t want to make prison sound easier than it was. The suffering was real. So pray also for comfort and endurance. They beat me; they broke my toe. But the prolonged separation from my two children was the hardest burden to bear. The day I went to prison, my son was 2 years old and my daughter was 7. Missing their childhoods was an unspeakable loss. Yet I know others who have suffered much more than I did. I think of a brother currently in prison who has been tortured. I think of a sister who was sexually assaulted when she was arrested. Even the apostle Paul was at times “so utterly burdened beyond [his] strength that [he] despaired of life itself.” And his request to the church was simple: “You also must help us by prayer” (2 Cor. 1:8, 11). Brothers and sisters like these need us to pray for them with love. Whatever the situation, we can pray that God would grant the suffering believer comfort, peace, and endurance. content: https://media.thegospelcoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/23102213/effective-evangelism.mp3 In the summer of 2021, pastor Luke Peterson moved to Columbus, Ohio, to look for lost people. To find them, he joined a gym. He started building friendships. And then he began asking those friends if they wanted to come over. “Word started getting around—‘You’re not going to believe this, but Luke’s a pastor,’” he said. ‘It created some intrigue, and people started coming. I used to have a note in my phone of how many people came to our church because I went to CrossFit Grandview. It was up to like 60 or 70 before I stopped counting because it was impossible.” Peterson’s good at evangelism, and his church is too—last year, they welcomed around 500 first-time visitors. When he preaches, he knows about half his audience is probably unchurched. Pastor Luke Peterson (right) chats with Capital Church attendees / Courtesy of Capital Church Facebook This is unusual in a country where 40 million adults have stopped attending church over the last 30 years, and where 76 percent of pastors said “fostering connections with unchurched people” is a need in their church. Much has changed since the Billy Graham rallies of the ’60s, the door-knocking of the ’80s, and seeker-sensitive church billboards of the ’90s. In the past, “you could randomly walk up to the person pumping gas next to you and say, ‘Do you know Jesus?’” said Perimeter Church pastor Jeff Norris. “Could that still work? Sure. But more and more, we tell people to invite neighbors into their home. The reality is that evangelism is much slower, and more relational, than it used to be.” Today, people aren’t as likely to read the Bible, think it’s the Word of God, or go to church . But they’re also less hostile to Christianity than they were five years ago. And while they read the Bible less—especially in Gen Z—the trajectory is moving up . “We’re not past ‘my truth, your truth,’” said Rob Warren, pastor of Doxa Church in Madison, Wisconsin. “But people aren’t as sure that their truth is actually true.” These days, evangelistically effective churches are keeping evangelism front of mind in the way they preach, train, and encourage their congregations. They’re celebrating small wins. And they’re leading with a high view of Scripture, prayer, and God’s sovereignty. “We’ve seen all of our ministries grow—from kids to youth to college ministry to Doxa Church as a whole,” Warren said. “It’s not just one demographic of people who are getting saved. God’s doing something.” Times Have Changed Thirty years ago, evangelical churches leaned on programs like Evangelism Explosion or Continuous Witness Training to deliver evangelistic focus and training, church leader Thom Rainer said . Those structured initiatives fit well in a culture that was more Christian and more institutionalized—it took an average of 20 church members to reach one person for Christ per year. Today, it takes 50, Rainer said . “Evangelism efficacy, evangelism effectiveness, has definitely diminished.” That trend is likely to continue. As social media and AI fill our time and increase our social anxiety, even relational evangelism is growing more difficult. title: We Need to Know Our Reformed Roots
summary: This volume is an invitation to rediscover that heritage and to find fresh encouragement in the faithfulness of God, who has sustained his church through the centuries.
summary_zh: 这本书邀请我们重新发现这一遗产，并在神的信实中找到新的鼓励，神几个世纪以来一直支持他的教会。
title_zh: 我们需要了解我们的改革根源
content: What does it mean to be Reformed? The label is used frequently but not always carefully. For some, it simply refers to a particular view of salvation. For others, it evokes a tradition, a culture, or even an aesthetic. Yet historically, to be Reformed has meant something much richer. While no single sentence can capture the fullness of the Reformed tradition, at minimum it means three things: to be biblical, to be covenantal, and to be confessional. The authority of Scripture governs our theology, covenant theology provides Scripture’s redemptive framework, and the historic confessions summarize and safeguard the church’s doctrinal convictions. Remove any one of those pillars, and something essential to the Reformed tradition is lost. With “Reformed” in its name, it’s hardly surprising that Reformed Theological Seminary has long sought to equip pastors and church members in all three areas. In recent years, members of its faculty have produced substantial volumes on the Old and New Testaments and on covenant theology. Now, with The Westminster Confession of Faith: A Comprehensive Commentary on Its History, Theology, and Application , they turn their attention to the confessional foundation of the Reformed tradition. The result is a volume that seeks not only to explain what the confession teaches but also to demonstrate why confessional theology remains vital for the church today. What Is the Westminster Confession of Faith? The Westminster Confession of Faith takes its name from the Westminster Assembly, a gathering of more than 100 ministers and theologians convened by the English Parliament in 1643 at a time of profound political and ecclesiastical upheaval. The assembly was tasked with recommending reforms to the doctrine, worship, government, and discipline of the Church of England. After more than five years of careful biblical study and theological deliberation, the assembly produced the Westminster Confession of Faith along with the Larger and Shorter Catechisms. Together, these documents have served as the doctrinal foundation of Presbyterian churches throughout the world for nearly four centuries. The assembly’s influence, however, extends far beyond Presbyterianism. The confession has helped shape the broader Reformed tradition, providing the framework for later confessional statements. As a result, its theological influence shaped generations of Congregationalists, Baptists, and other evangelical Christians. The editors of this volume rightly observe, The confession is also ecumenical because it found wide acceptance among Congregationalists and Particular Baptists in the seventeenth century, as two different groups of theologians adapted the confession according to their theological convictions, producing the Savoy Declaration (1658) and the Second London Confession (1689). Thus the Westminster Confession is relevant to Presbyterians, Congregationalists, and Baptists. (xx) Why Another Commentary? The Westminster Confession has never lacked commentators. From the 17th century onward, pastors and theologians have written to explain its theology. Quality works by A. A. Hodge , G. I. Williamson, R. C. Sproul, and more recently Chad Van Dixhoorn have each served the church well in different ways. So why do we need another commentary on the confession, and what makes this one useful? The Westminster Confession has helped shape the broader Reformed tradition, providing the framework for later confessional statements. First, this isn’t the work of a single author but a collaborative effort by scholars whose expertise spans several areas of theology. That breadth allows the volume to approach the confession from different perspectives while maintaining a clear unity of purpose. Each contributor brings particular expertise to the section he addresses, but the volume as a whole is concerned with helping readers understand the confession and its significance for the church. Second, the commentary is consciously pastoral. Rath
content_zh: 改革意味着什么? 标签经常使用,但并不总是谨慎。 对某些人来说,它只是提到救赎的特定观点. 对其他人来说,它引起一种传统、一种文化,甚至一种美学。 然而,从历史上看,改革意味着更加富有的东西。 虽然没有一句话能捕捉到被改造后的传统的全部,但至少它意味着三件事:是圣经,是盟约,是忏悔. 圣经的权威支配着我们的神学,盟约神学提供了圣经的红发框架,历史的忏悔总结并捍卫了教会的教义信念。 移除其中任何一根支柱,失去对改革后的传统至关重要的东西。 改革神学院长期试图在所有三个领域为牧师和教会成员提供教具, 近年来,该校院士编写了大量关于"旧约"和"新约"和"盟约神学"等著作. 现在,随着《威斯敏斯特信仰的忏悔:对其历史、神学和适用的综合评论》,他们把注意力转向改革后传统的忏悔基础。 结果的一卷不仅试图解释忏悔的教义,还试图表明为什么忏悔神学在今天仍然对教会至关重要. 韦斯敏斯特对信仰的忏悔是什么? 威斯敏斯特信仰忏悔会取而代之的是威斯敏斯特大会(Westminster Assembly),这是1643年英国议会在政治与教会剧变深刻的时期召开的由100多位部长和神学家组成的集会. 大会的任务是建议对英格兰教会的学说,崇拜,政府和纪律进行改革. 经过五年多的认真的圣经研究和神学审议后,大会产生了"威斯敏斯特信仰忏悔"(Westminster Confession of Faith)和"更大规模和更短的卡特克主义". 近四个世纪以来,这些文件共同成为全世界长老会教会的理论基础。 然而,议会的影响远远超出长老会。 忏悔有助于形成更广泛的改革后传统,为后来的忏悔声明提供了框架。 因此,它的神学影响塑造了几代基督教会,浸信会等福音派基督徒. 这本书的编辑们正确地指出,《忏悔书》也具有普世性,因为它在17世纪被基督教会和特定浸信会广泛接受,因为两个不同的神学家群体根据他们的神学信念修改了供词,产生了"萨伏依宣言"(1658年)和"第二次伦敦忏悔书"(1689年). 因此,威斯敏斯特忏悔与长老会、基督教会和浸信会有关。 (二十) 为什么另作一评注? 威斯敏斯特的"忏悔"从未缺少评论家. 从17世纪起,牧师和神学家都撰文解释其神学. A. A. Hodge、G. I. Williamson、R. C. Sproul和最近的Chad Van Dixhoorn以不同方式为教堂服务。 因此,我们为什么需要关于供词的另一条评论,是什么使得这一条有用呢? 威斯敏斯特忏悔有助于形成更广泛的改革后传统,为后来的忏悔声明提供了框架. 首先,这不是一位作者的工作,而是学者的合作努力,他们的专业知识跨越了神学的几个领域。 这种宽度允许量从不同的角度对待供词,同时保持明确的目的一致。 每个贡献者都会为他所讲的一节带来特殊的专门知识,但该卷整体关注的是帮助读者理解忏悔及其对教会的意义. 第二,评注是自觉的放肆。 拉斯语Name

title: If the Church Did Its Job, Would the Parachurch Exist?
summary: Do pregnancy centers, food pantries, or campus ministries exist because the church is failing to do her work?
summary_zh: 是否存在怀孕中心、食品储藏室或校园事工，因为教会未能完成她的工作？
title_zh: 如果教会做了它的工作，教堂会存在吗？
content: I’ve heard it said more than once: “If the church did its job, the parachurch wouldn’t have to exist.” For instance, I was consulting with a local pastor who wanted to see the church serve people in poverty in his community. It was important to him that the church do it, not a nonprofit. Since he understood that God’s kingdom is bigger than his congregation, he wanted to engage multiple churches in the project. I suggested he consider forming a council of pastors and collectively hiring a staff member to manage the operations of the combined program. He thought that could work well for his context. I’m not sure he was aware of the irony. I certainly was: We’d just reinvented a variant of the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that he so keenly wanted to avoid in the first place. While the allergy to faith-based nonprofits was especially strong in his case, many people accept the premise at a basic level. In my experience, this sentiment is just as likely to come from someone who works in nonchurch ministry as from a pastor. If we understand the church is the core institution created by Christ to advance the kingdom of heaven, has it failed so badly that we need an army of auxiliaries to prop it up? Clarifying Terms and Roles I answer that the parachurch doesn’t exist because the church has failed. It exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. Proving that starts with clarifying terms. The parachurch exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. “Church” has more than one use in Scripture. In some contexts, it describes the people of God universally (Matt. 16:15–18; Eph. 1:22–23; Col. 1:18). In others, it’s a local congregational institution with the parameters God has placed around its operation (1 Thess. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3:1–5; Philem. 1:2; James 5:14). “Parachurch” typically refers to faith-based nonprofits who serve people in need or provide evangelistic and discipleship resources. Certainly, as part of the universal church, all God’s people hold equal status in advancing God’s mission, whether they labor as nurses, students, pastors, or tentmakers (see Acts 18:1–3). Just as surely, all God’s people shouldn’t merely attend but be accountable to a local congregation that enables their spiritual formation. When not assembled, God’s people are charged with many tasks—everything from stewarding creation to seeking justice for the oppressed. We can fulfill these tasks as individuals, but it often makes sense to create or join institutions dedicated to fulfilling them. Which brings us to a crucial point: God ordained some institutions specifically, and some emerged organically from God’s commands. Ordained or Emergent Institutions The family, the local church, and the government are ordained institutions. The Bible gives each ordained institution some guidance but also leaves a lot open to interpretation. While these ordained institutions are necessary for all people, they aren’t sufficient to fulfill God’s myriad commands to their fullest extent. Thus, some institutions emerge from the commands, rather than from a revealed institutional structure: The command to work led to the formation of businesses. The command to pass knowledge to subsequent generations led to the formation of schools. The command to care for the sick caused Christians to form the first hospitals. The command to care for the poor, widows, orphans, and strangers led to the formation of charities . The command to make disciples of all nations led to mission boards, publishing houses, and Bible-translation ministries. This ordained-emergent distinction parallels Abraham Kuyper’s “ sphere sovereignty ” in its recognition of institutions not explicitly outlined in Scripture. Many of these commands can be fulfilled to some lesser degree by the ordained institutions, but there are limitations. A family may work without forming a business, but they’ll never raise a skyscraper. Most be

title: Ministry Lessons from the Puritans (with Joel Beeke)
summary: Joel Beeke joins Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan to explore what the Puritans can teach today’s pastors about prayer, preaching, personal holiness, shepherding souls, handling criticism, and persevering in ministry.
summary_zh: 乔尔·比克（ Joel Beeke ）与马特·斯梅瑟斯特（ Matt Smethurst ）和利贡·邓肯（ Ligon Duncan ）一起探索清教徒可以教导今天的牧师关于祈祷、讲道、个人圣洁、牧养灵魂、处理批评和坚持传道。
title_zh: 清教徒的教训（与Joel Beeke一起）
content: What can pastors today learn from the Puritans? Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan welcome Joel Beeke to discuss the lasting wisdom of Puritan pastors and theologians. Drawing from decades of studying and teaching the Puritans, Beeke explains why they placed such a high priority on prayer, personal holiness, and applying Scripture to the hearts and lives of their congregations. title: Art Programs in Lebanon Bring Beauty to Midst of Crisis
summary: With Lebanon currently being impacted by war, a refugee crisis, and more, stories of beauty can be hard to come across. For ministries active in Lebanon, meeting the spiritual, physical...
summary_zh: 由于黎巴嫩目前受到战争、难民危机等的影响，美丽的故事可能很难被理解。对于在黎巴嫩活跃的事工，满足精神，物质...
title_zh: 黎巴嫩的艺术项目将美丽带入危机
content: With Lebanon currently being impacted by war, a refugee crisis, and more, stories of beauty can be hard to come across. For ministries active in Lebanon, meeting the spiritual, physical and emotional needs of a country just trying to survive can take its toll. Horizons International’s Pierre Houssney said that despite the trauma the country faces due to the fallenness of man in a sinful world, God has still created a world that contains beauty. “And I think that beauty speaks to people’s hearts about God, especially when it’s not just beauty, you know, for beauty’s sake, but when it’s beauty in the name of Christ,” Houssney said. “In the midst of the trauma, in the midst of the poverty, we’re trying to give opportunities for believers, who have artistic gifts, to have a prophetic voice through their art to the society, so that we can be calling out for Christ in the midst of the crisis.” Some of these opportunities for creating beauty are fine art classes offered by Horizons International. Horizons International has had up to 35 students at one time participating in these classes revolving around painting or drawing. Students in visual arts classes had the opportunity to participate in an exhibition in Beirut called “His Touch.” People from the community were invited to see the work of beginner students as well as 10 different Christian artists. Graphic design classes offer a more practical element, allowing students to learn a skill they could use in their everyday lives. On the worship side of things, music theory and classes in instruments are helping raise up worship leaders for local churches. One unit teaching guitar, piano, and drums to beginners looking to lead worship at their church had 70 people participate. “And so this new generation needs training, and they need, you know, they need mentoring, and they need to have those skills so that they can, they can lead their congregations in worship,” Houssney said. Though some may have more trouble connecting visual arts directly with ministry, Houssney says social media helps make that connection more clear. Beautiful videos that contain scripture messages alongside visual art tend to get a higher viewership. When posts like that get more views, they can potentially bring more people to Christ. “And so it needs to be beautiful. It needs to be excellent, it needs to be well done. And that’s what our Lord deserves,” Houssney said. “That’s not just what social media deserves.” Currently, Horizons International has to spread resources between humanitarian aid like food and medicine and projects that glorify God through the arts. In the midst of the crisis in Lebanon, pray for God to provide the resources for canvases, studio spaces, art instructors and more. Houssney also says what an organization like Horizons International is here for is to see God open more and more hearts to the Gospel. “So I’m not praying that the church would have less hardship. I’m not praying for you know, for less, you know, political chaos. What I’m praying for is that, through it all, people would continue to open their hearts, and that God will be glorified.” Learn more about the work of Horizons International in Lebanon by visiting https://www.horizonsinternational.org/lebanon-crisis .
content_zh: 黎巴嫩目前受到战争、难民危机等影响, 对活跃在黎巴嫩的各部来说,满足一个国家的精神、身体和情感需求,只是为了生存而努力,这可能会造成损失。 Horizons International的Pierre Houssney说,尽管由于人类在罪恶世界中的堕落,国家仍然面临创伤,但上帝仍然创造了一个包含美丽的世界。 “我认为,美丽对人们的心来说是关于上帝的,特别是当它不仅仅是为美丽着想,而是以基督为名的美丽时,”Houssney说。 “在创伤中,在贫困中,我们试图给那些拥有艺术天赋的信徒机会,通过他们的艺术向社会发出先知的声音,以便在危机中呼唤基督。” 其中一些创造美貌的机会是地平线国际提供的精美艺术课. 地平线国际曾经有多达35名学生参加这些围绕绘画或绘画而旋转的课. 视觉艺术课的学生有机会在贝鲁特参加一个名为“他的触摸”的展览。 社区人士被邀请观看初学者和10名不同的基督教艺术家的作品. 图形设计课程提供了更实用的元素,让学生学习在日常生活中可以使用的技能. 在事物的崇拜方面,乐器中的音乐理论和课程正在帮助培养地方教会的崇拜领袖. 一个教吉他,钢琴,和鼓的单位在他们的教堂里为初学者寻找引领崇拜,有70人参加. “因此,这新一代需要培训,他们需要,你知道,他们需要指导,他们需要这些技能,以便他们能够领导他们的教会进行礼拜。” 虽然有些人可能更难直接将视觉艺术与部委联系起来, 包含经文信息与视觉艺术的美丽视频往往获得更高的收视率. 当这样的帖子获得更多的观点时,它们有可能将更多的人带入基督. “因此,它必须是美丽的。 它需要出色,需要做得很好。 这才是我们的主应得的。 这不仅仅是社交媒体应得的。 目前,地平线国际必须在食品和医药等人道主义援助和通过艺术来赞美上帝的项目之间分配资源。 在黎巴嫩危机中,祈求上帝为画布、工作室空间、艺术教员等提供资源。 霍斯尼还说,像地平线国际这样的组织在这里是为了看到上帝对"福音"越来越开放的心. 我并不祈祷教会会减少困难。 我并不是为你们祈祷, 我所祈祷的是,通过这一切,人们将继续敞开心扉,而上帝将受到赞美。” 透过访问https://www.horisonsinternational.org/lebanon-crisis,

title: Abide
summary: This incident took place over 15 years ago, and yet, I remember it clearly. In the buzz of daily life, it is easy to get caught up in the carelessness...
summary_zh: 这件事发生在15年前，但我记得很清楚。在日常生活的嗡嗡声中，很容易陷入粗心大意……
title_zh: v.容忍
content: This incident took place over 15 years ago, and yet, I remember it clearly.  In the buzz of daily life, it is easy to get caught up in the carelessness of the checklists, and forget the intentionality of abiding in Him. I remember how frantic I was once at or late deadline and how frustrated I was at all the problems we were having in getting the program together.  We’d all kinds of equipment failure throughout the day and I was going to have to drive the program across town to get it uploaded to the satellite.  It was already 7 pm and the babysitter was calling me every 10 minutes. Then, I got a call from a lady with a gentle Creole accent. She told me, “I felt led to call you and pray with you.”  I SO didn’t want to talk to this lady, wasn’t interested in being prayed over, and really just wanted to leave to get this program fed and pick my 2-year old up.  I was impatient when I responded to her.  Rather than take insult from what was probably a curt rebuff,  she just said , “Wow. You REALLY need the peace of our heavenly Father on your heart right now.” And…she burst out in song.   Now I’m wondering why I’m on the phone with this crazy lady, and then she prayed through the worship song and then rolled right into praying for me, for my distress, for the things I thought I needed to do…and prayed that I would be still and listen, that my heart would be quiet long enough to remember the awe of God, and that the joy would come back to my heart as we produced MNN… The more she prayed, the more convicted I grew and I realized I was caught up in the ‘do’ and not the ‘be’…and THEN she pulled out the big guns: the story of Mary and Martha. Luke 10:38-42 New International Version (NIV) At the Home of Martha and Mary 38 As Jesus and his disciples were on their way, he came to a village where a woman named Martha opened her home to him. 39 She had a sister called Mary, who sat at the Lord’s feet listening to what he said. 40 But Martha was distracted by all the preparations that had to be made. She came to him and asked, “Lord, don’t you care that my sister has left me to do the work by myself? Tell her to help me!” 41 “Martha, Martha,” the Lord answered, “you are worried and upset about many things, 42 but few things are needed—or indeed only one. [ a ] Mary has chosen what is better, and it will not be taken away from her.” She ended our conversation with, “Sometimes, it’s ok to be Mary and sit at the feet of Jesus.  Stuff will still be there to do. It will eventually get done.  But the lasting investment is remembering to sit and BE at the feet of Jesus.” It was a much needed gentle rebuke along with a little encouragement from an unknown sister in Christ that I still remember to this day…thousands of productions later.   What we do is important…but not at the risk of forgetting to abide in Christ.
content_zh: 这一事件发生在15多年前,然而,我清楚地记得。 在日常生活中,很容易陷入清单的粗心大意之中,而忘记遵守他的意向。 我记得我曾经在最后期限或晚到的时候 多么疯狂 以及我对我们把节目整理好时遇到的所有问题 感到多么沮丧 我将不得不把程序推向全城, 已经七点了 保姆每十分钟给我打电话 然后,我接到一个女士的电话 带着温柔的克里奥尔口音。 她对我说:我的确猜想,我曾与你一起祈祷。 我本不想和这位女士交谈, 我对她的反应很不耐烦 她没有从可能是一种曲折的反驳中取出侮辱,而是说,“哇。 你现在真的需要我们天父的和平。” 然后... 她唱出歌来 她透过崇拜之歌祈祷, 然后转而为我祈祷, 为我的痛苦祈祷, 祈祷我需要做的事情. 她越是祈祷, 我越是被定罪, Luke 10:38-42 新国际版 (NIV) 在玛莎和玛丽38的家,由于耶稣和他的门徒们在路上,他来到一个村庄,一个叫玛莎的女人向他打开了她的家. 39 她有一个叫玛丽的姐姐,她坐在主的脚下,听他说的话。 40,但玛莎被所有必须做的准备所分心. 她来到他身边问道,“主啊,你难道不关心我姐姐离开我一个人做这个工作吗? " 41 " Martha, Martha, " 主回答说, " 你对许多事情感到担心和不安,42件,但需要的东西很少,甚至只有一件。 [a] 玛利亚已选择了更好的事物,它不会被夺走。 她结束我们的谈话时, 事情还会在那里做。 它最终会完成。 但持久的投资是记得坐在耶稣的脚下。” 这是非常需要的温柔的回斥 以及基督中一个未知的妹妹的一点鼓励 我至今仍然记得... 我们所做的是重要的... 但不会冒着忘记遵守基督的风险

title: Koinonia
summary: Koinonia (Koy-no-nee’-ah) is a Greek word, occurring 20 times in the Bible, which means “fellowship” or “brotherly love.” It carries with it the meaning of a committed, trustworthy, and dependable...
summary_zh: Koinonia （ Koy-no-nee '-ah ）是一个希腊语单词，在圣经中出现了20次，意思是“团契”或“兄弟之爱”。“它带有忠诚、值得信赖和可靠的意义……
title_zh: Koinonia
content: Koinonia (Koy-no-nee’-ah) is a Greek word, occurring 20 times in the Bible, which means “fellowship” or “brotherly love.” It carries with it the meaning of a committed, trustworthy, and dependable relationship. Such a relationship can be experienced through participation, sharing, giving, and contributing. The first occurrence of koinonia is Acts 2:42 “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and to the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.” But the rest of the passage reads:  “ 43 Everyone was filled with awe at the many wonders and signs performed by the apostles. 44 All the believers were together and had everything in common. 45 They sold property and possessions to give to anyone who had need. 46 Every day they continued to meet together in the temple courts. They broke bread in their homes and ate together with glad and sincere hearts, 47 praising God and enjoying the favor of all the people. And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.” Christian fellowship is a key aspect of the Christian life. Believers in Christ are to come together in love, faith, and encouragement. The essence of koinonia: “one another”. Scripture commands us to be devoted to one another (Romans 12:10), honor one another (Romans 12:10), live in harmony with one another (Romans 12:16; 1 Peter 3:8), accept one another (Romans 15:7), serve one another in love (Galatians 5:13), be kind and compassionate to one another (Ephesians 4:32), admonish one another (Colossians 3:16), encourage one another (1 Thessalonians 5:11; Hebrews 3:13), spur one another on toward love and good deeds (Hebrews 10:24), offer hospitality (1 Peter 4:9), and love one another (1 Peter 1:22; 1 John 3:11; 3:23; 4:7; 4:11-12). Koinonia is translated many different ways in English Bibles: -fellowship (koinonia), to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” -contribution (koinonia) for them and for all others.” Paul writes to the believers in Philippi: “That I may know him and the power of his resurrection, and may share (koinonia) his sufferings, becoming like him in his death” (Phil 3:10). – Christian living– the dynamic whole of it. It describes an interactive relationship between God and believers who are sharing new life through Christ.  It captures the entirety of this relationship. It involves active participation in Christian community: sharing in spiritual blessings and giving material blessings. How does this idea fit into the theology of ‘And’? Acts 1:8—it empowers us with the chisomo—the grace to DO—the all-inclusive– “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes on you; and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.” And they will know you by your love.  (John 13:35)   “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you love one another.”

title: Covenant
summary: Isaiah 54:10 Though the mountains be shaken and the hills be removed, yet my unfailing love for you will not be shaken nor my covenant of peace be removed,” says...
summary_zh: Isaiah 54:10大山虽摇动，小山虽迁移，我对你们永不止息的爱却不摇动，我平安的约也不迁移。”
title_zh: 契  约
content: Isaiah 54:10  Though the mountains be shaken and the hills be removed, yet my unfailing love for you will not be shaken nor my covenant of peace be removed,” says the LORD, who has compassion on you. There is something of music in the very sound of these words. The thought that lies below them, sweeping as it does through the whole creation, and parting all things into the transient and eternal, the mortal and immortal, is still greater than the music of the words. ‘These’ are removed; ‘this’ abides. The thing in God which abides is all-gentle tenderness, that strange love mightier than all the powers of Deity beside, permanent with the permanence of His changeless heart. ‘My loving kindness and the covenant of My peace,’ outlast everything else. The antithesis of what passes and what abides is mind-boggling. ‘all things are in a state of flux’—it’s a basic tenant of physical science…and yet it seems as unchanging as anything we know…it’s the shape of the box…and yet,  if we had nothing abiding beyond this universe, what would be the point? There’s an unspoken  ‘But’  here–  in that vacuum, the Great Spirit moves all the material universe, Himself unmoved, undiminished by creation, or by said vacuum.  The Unknowable whose name means ‘breath’ is YHWH—who comes to us in man-form to help the created move toward and abide in this presence. I’m sort of blown away by how big this passage paints God…and blown away that we are His children…and that we able to abide because of Christ…that our part in glorifying Him and enjoying Him forever comes in walking alongside a global family and telling their stories.  Insignificant, by itself, but being used as a tool to help others abide and recognize the mercy and grace of this big Abba. We can touch the face of God…because He calls us to Himself.

title: Innocent As Doves
summary: The Scriptures Ephesians 6:10-18 (NIV) 10 Finally, be strong in the Lord and in his mighty power. 11 Put on the full armor of God, so that you can take...
summary_zh: 以弗所书6:10 -18 （ NIV ） 10最后，靠着主和祂的大能要坚强。11穿上神的全副军装，这样你就可以……
title_zh: Innocent As Doves
content: The Scriptures Ephesians 6:10-18 (NIV) 10 Finally, be strong in the Lord and in his mighty power. 11 Put on the full armor of God, so that you can take your stand against the devil’s schemes. 12 For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this dark world and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms. 13 Therefore put on the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you may be able to stand your ground, and after you have done everything, to stand. 14 Stand firm then, with the belt of truth buckled around your waist, with the breastplate of righteousness in place, 15 and with your feet fitted with the readiness that comes from the gospel of peace. 16 In addition to all this, take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one. 17 Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit,which is the word of God. 18 And pray in the Spirit on all occasions with all kinds of prayers and requests. With this in mind, be alert and always keep on praying for all the Lord’s people. Matthew 10:16-20 16 “I am sending you out like sheep among wolves. Therefore be as shrewd as snakes and as innocent as doves. 17 Be on your guard; you will be handed over to the local councils and be flogged in the synagogues. 18 On my account you will be brought before governors and kings as witnesses to them and to the Gentiles.19 But when they arrest you, do not worry about what to say or how to say it. At that time you will be given what to say, 20 for it will not be you speaking, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.” Today, it’s just been on my mind to bring our attention back to the armor of God and the fact we need to be wise like serpents, innocent as doves. I want to speak to the first part, being wise like serpents. Going to Malta helped bring to my attention how much I don’t know about my own country’s politics, the refugee crisis, trusting God, and even God’s word. I feel like I’m doing “better than the average U.S. citizen.” But, in reality, I don’t know very much. And I’ve realized when it comes to engaging in conversation with others, it’s important to have a handle on topics like these. I.e., talking with my dad about refugees. Having facts and knowing the what the constitution says helps me to better articulate and defend my stance culturally and based by our country’s laws. Knowing about the situation with refugees abroad also helps and is a tool in dispelling the fear which the current administration seems to use to get support to make the calls it’s trying to make both about refugees and immigrants in general. The second part, being innocent like doves…that’s a hard one for me because I’ve thought in the past it means to be naive. I don’t want to be naïve. But being innocent doesn’t mean you’re naïve. I think it means we guard our hearts and take our thoughts captive. What we put into our minds affects the lens through which we see the world and view the Bible—and it has the power to jade us. I.e., rape. I know rape is in the world. I know it is destructive. I’ve seen it damage lives. And I’ve seen God redeem. But, what I don’t need to do is read the part of a book or watch a TV series which details a situation of rape. I don’t need to invite that in my mind to “know” about rape. I’m thinking of a book one of my youth group girls was reading. I haven’t read it, but I see how she struggles with her sexuality, her relationship with God, and for a period even suicide. I also see how her parents are okay with exposing her to things that are a bit mature for her age. Compared to another one of our girls who is aware of what happens in the world, but her parents are careful to protect her from exposure to things which are dark, damaging, fracture her relationship with God. She’s being taught to be innocent, not naïve (or judgmental), and to take her thoughts captive. Both of these
content_zh: 圣经以弗所书: 6: 10-18(NIV) 10 最后,要坚固于主和他强大的力量. 11 穿上上帝的全盔甲,以便你能够采取立场对抗魔鬼的阴谋. 12,因为我们的斗争不是反对血肉之争,而是反对统治者,反对当局,反对这个黑暗世界的力量,反对天界邪恶的精神力量. 13 因此穿上神的全甲,使出恶事之日到来后能站起地来,在做了一切后能站起地来. 14 站稳了, 真理带系住你的腰部, 胸罩是正义的, 15 和你的脚 与来自和平的福音的准备。 16,除此外,取起信道之盾,用之能灭一切恶道所发之火箭. 17取出救生之盔和"灵剑",这是"神之道". 18,并随各种祷告和请求,在"精神"中作各种祈祷. 考虑到这一点,保持警惕,并始终为主的所有人民祈祷。 Matthew 10:16-20 16 “我把你像羊一样放出狼群。 因此要像蛇一样精明,像鸽子一样无辜. 17 个 人 守 住 ; 交给 地方 议会 、 在 犹太会堂 被 鞭打 . 18,就我而言,你们将被带见总督和国王,作为他们和外邦人的见证。 19,但当他们逮捕你时,不要担心该说什么或怎么说. 在那日,你们得享受你们所应当享受的,20个是你们所应当享受的,只有你们父亲的精神。 今天,我刚刚想到让我们重新关注上帝的盔甲, 以及我们需要像蛇一样聪明, 我想谈谈第一部分,像蛇一样聪明。 前往马耳他让我注意到我对本国政治、难民危机、信任上帝甚至上帝之言一无所知。 我觉得自己比普通美国公民做得更好。 但事实上, 我意识到在与他人对话时, 和我爸谈难民的事 了解事实、了解宪法内容, 有助于我更好地表达和捍卫我的立场, 了解国外难民的情况,也有助于消除现政府似乎用来获得支持的恐惧, 第二部分是像鸽子一样无辜, 我不想天真。 但无辜并不意味着你天真。 我认为这意味着我们保护我们的心 并抓住我们的思想。 我们脑中的东西影响着我们通过这个镜头看到世界并看到圣经——它有制玉的力量。 强奸 我知道强奸在世界上。 我知道这是破坏性的。 我见过它会伤害生命。 我见过上帝赎回。 但我不需要阅读一本书或看一部电视连续剧, 我并不需要邀请她「知道」强奸事件。 我想到一本我的青年团体女孩正在阅读的书。 我还没读过, 但我看到她如何与性、与上帝的关系相抗争, 我也明白她的父母 让她面对一些对她的年龄来说有点成熟的事情是怎样的 和另外一位我们的女孩相比,她知道世界发生的事情,但她的父母很小心地保护她免受那些黑暗,有破坏力,断裂她与上帝关系的东西的暴露. 她被教导自己是无辜的, 两者

summary_zh: 创世记第13章于是亚伯兰离开埃及，带着他的妻子和罗得以及他们所拥有的一切，向北进入内盖夫。2 （亚伯兰的牲畜非常丰富， ……
title_zh: 亚伯拉罕和洛特
content: Genesis 13 So Abram left Egypt and traveled north into the Negev, along with his wife and Lot and all that they owned. 2 (Abram was very rich in livestock, silver, and gold.) 3 From the Negev, they continued traveling by stages toward Bethel, and they pitched their tents between Bethel and Ai, where they had camped before. 4 This was the same place where Abram had built the altar, and there he worshiped the Lord again. 5 Lot, who was traveling with Abram, had also become very wealthy with flocks of sheep and goats, herds of cattle, and many tents. 6 But the land could not support both Abram and Lot with all their flocks and herds living so close together. 7 So disputes broke out between the herdsmen of Abram and Lot. (At that time Canaanites and Perizzites were also living in the land.) 8 Finally Abram said to Lot, “Let’s not allow this conflict to come between us or our herdsmen. After all, we are close relatives! 9 The whole countryside is open to you. Take your choice of any section of the land you want, and we will separate. If you want the land to the left, then I’ll take the land on the right. If you prefer the land on the right, then I’ll go to the left.” 10 Lot took a long look at the fertile plains of the Jordan Valley in the direction of Zoar. The whole area was well watered everywhere, like the garden of the Lord or the beautiful land of Egypt. (This was before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.) 11 Lot chose for himself the whole Jordan Valley to the east of them. He went there with his flocks and servants and parted company with his uncle Abram. 12 So Abram settled in the land of Canaan, and Lot moved his tents to a place near Sodom and settled among the cities of the plain. 13 But the people of this area were extremely wicked and constantly sinned against the Lord. 14 After Lot had gone, the Lord said to Abram, “Look as far as you can see in every direction—north and south, east and west. 15 I am giving all this land, as far as you can see, to you and your descendants[a] as a permanent possession. 16 And I will give you so many descendants that, like the dust of the earth, they cannot be counted! 17 Go and walk through the land in every direction, for I am giving it to you.” 18 So Abram moved his camp to Hebron and settled near the oak grove belonging to Mamre. There he built another altar to the Lord. At this point in the story, God’s promise to Abraham of the promised land hasn’t come true yet, but good land is part of the promise We’ve seen Abraham have faithful triumphs and failures, but this is a time when Abraham showed great faith once again because there are SEVERAL reasons why Abraham could have taken the better land 1. movement towards God’s promise of good land anyway 2. and this is probably a more striking one to me, but culturally speaking, the older would NEVER defer to the younger. Lot, as the younger, should have deferred to Abraham the older – both in going to him to resolve the disagreement between their herdsmen and in giving him the better pick of land But Abraham wasn’t fixated on culture and on manipulating God’s promises Abraham’s dealings are not in seniority, but in brotherly love and that’s what faith does. Faith resolves tension with generous self-sacrifice Christians often say in tense situations, “Well, I’m not a doormat! I deserve not to be walked all over!” But my pastor said something very striking to me. “Aren’t we glad Christ never said that?” A faithful and generous person doesn’t need to manipulate or control the situation because they are resting in the promises and sovereignty of God Faith leads to trust leads to generosity and self-sacrifice with others.
content_zh: 创世记13 索·阿布拉姆从埃及出走,向北走入了内盖夫河,与他的妻子和洛特以及他们所拥有的一切. 2 (Abram有非常丰富的牲畜,白银和黄金. 3 他们从内盖夫出发,继续分步向贝瑟尔出行,在贝瑟尔和艾之间搭起帐篷,他们以前在那里扎营. 页:1 这是阿布拉姆建造祭坛的地方,在那里他再次崇拜了主. 5,当时正与阿布拉姆一起出行的洛特也变得非常富有了有羊羊群,牛群和许多帐篷. 6个 但土地无法支撑阿布拉姆和洛特 他们所有的羊群和群 生活如此相近。 第7条 亞伯蘭和魯特的牧民,互相爭論; (當時,迦南人和比瑞斯人同住), 8 最后,Abram对Lot说: " 让我们不要让这场冲突发生在我们和牧民之间。 我们毕竟是近亲! 第9条 整个农村都对你开放. 你选择你想要的土地的任何部分 我们就会分开 如果你想让土地在左边,那我就让土地在右边。 如果你喜欢右边的土地,那么我就往左边去。 10 洛特对约旦河谷向左尔方向的肥沃平原进行了长时间的考察. 整个地区到处都有良好的取水,如主的花园或埃及美丽的地. (这是在主毁灭了索多玛和戈莫拉之前) 11 洛特自己选择了他们以东的整个约旦河谷. 他带着他的羊群和仆人去那儿,和他叔叔Abram分道扬镳。 12日,阿布拉姆在迦南地定居,洛特将帐篷搬到了索多姆附近的一个地方,并定居于平地的城市中. 13,但此地之人,极恶而常犯主. 14 在洛特离开后,主对Abram说: " 请你看看每一个方向,即北和南、东和西。 15,我把所有的土地,就你所看到的,作为永久财产,交给你和你的子孙。 十六,我给你这么多的后人,像地上的尘土一样,他们不能被统计! 17 出行,走遍地上,各行各业,我把它赏赐你们。” 18日,阿布拉姆将营地迁至希伯伦并定居在属于马姆雷的橡树林附近. 在那里他又为主建造了一座祭坛. 在故事的这一刻,上帝对亚伯拉罕的允诺还没有实现,但好地是我们所见到的亚伯拉罕有忠实的胜利和失败的诺言的一部分,但此时亚伯拉罕再次表现出了极大的信心,因为有SEVERAL的理由,亚伯拉罕可以夺取更好的地一. 但从文化上讲, 年长者决不会屈从于年轻人。 作为年轻人,洛特应该把年长者留给亚伯拉罕 — — 既去他解决牧民之间的分歧,又让他选择更好的土地 — — 但亚伯拉罕并不热衷于文化和操纵上帝对亚伯拉罕的诺言 — — 亚伯拉罕的交往不是在资历上,而是在兄弟般的爱心上,而这正是信仰的作用。 信仰用慷慨自救的基督徒解决了紧张局势, 我不应该到处走! 但我的牧师对我说了一些非常引人注目的话。 “难道我们不庆幸基督从未这么说吗?” 一个忠诚而慷慨的人不需要操控或控制局势,因为他们沉浸在上帝信仰的承诺中,而主权导致信任导致与他人的慷慨和自我牺牲。
